title: Fundamental limits of parameter estimation with heralded optical non-Gaussian states generated from Gaussian resources
authors: Shohei Kiryu, Kazufumi Tanji, Yoshihiro Ueda, Kosuke Fukui, Masahiro Takeoka
abstract: Non-Gaussian states can exhibit large quantum Fisher information (QFI) in quantum sensing. In optical systems, however, its generation is often probabilistic via the boson-sampling type conditional operation and thus its generation rate is limited. This probabilistic generation of non-Gaussian resource should be taken into account for evaluation of the sensing performance. Then a natural question arising is whether the use of heralded probabilistic non-Gaussian states is better than that of the original deterministic Gaussian states for quantum sensing. In this paper, we answer to this question for single-parameter phase-estimation. By using photon-number conservation in passive linear optical systems, we show that heralded state preparation before parameter encoding can be mapped to a postselection problem after parameter encoding for phase estimation. This mapping allows the success probability of heralding to be included naturally in the metrological performance. We introduce an effective quantum Fisher information (EQFI), defined as the success-probability-weighted QFI of the heralded outputs, and prove that it cannot exceed the QFI of the original Gaussian inputs. The result highlights the importance of resource counting in quantum sensing toward better understanding of the resource efficient advantage of optical quantum sensing.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the fundamental limits of phase estimation using heralded non-Gaussian states generated from Gaussian resources in optical systems. By defining an Effective Quantum Fisher Information (EQFI) that weights by success probability, the authors prove that this resource cannot surpass the QFI limit set by the original deterministic Gaussian input state. This highlights the critical importance of accounting for generation efficiency in quantum metrology.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether using heralded, probabilistic non-Gaussian quantum states offers a genuine metrological advantage over deterministic Gaussian states for single-parameter phase estimation.
main_result: It is proven that the Effective Quantum Fisher Information (EQFI) of the heralded non-Gaussian states cannot exceed the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) achievable with the original Gaussian input state, when resource cost (success probability) is accounted for.
method: The authors define and calculate the EQFI as a success-probability-weighted average of the conditional QFI over all possible detection outcomes from photon number resolving detectors.
model_or_system: The analysis uses passive linear optical circuits acting on Gaussian input states (like squeezed vacuum) to generate heralded non-Gaussian states, with phase estimation performed by applying a global phase rotation operator.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), Effective Quantum Fisher Information (EQFI), Success Probability ($P(n_B)$).
important_parameters: The comparison is between $	ext{EQFI}$ and the input $	ext{QFI}$, particularly in regimes involving photon number conservation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes linear phase estimation using passive linear optics, and crucially incorporates the success probability of the heralding process into the performance metric.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate quantum sensing schemes comparing non-Gaussian vs. Gaussian states, showing how the probabilistic nature (heralding) is mapped to an effective measurement strategy.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a formal mapping between heralded state preparation and postselection after parameter encoding. It then derives the EQFI metric and proves the upper bound ($	ext{EQFI} \le 	ext{QFI}_{	ext{input}}$), using commutation relations to justify this result.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous resource-counting benchmark for quantum sensing, showing that mere non-Gaussianity is insufficient for advantage if generation probabilities are ignored in linear optics settings.
